sections.title: The Eastern Tribes Return Home
observations: After the conquest of Canaan, the tribes of Reuben, Gad, and the half-tribe of Manasseh were given permission to return to their land east of the Jordan River. This decision was made after they had fulfilled their commitment to help the other tribes in battle. Their return signifies the importance of keeping promises and the unity among the tribes of Israel.

sections.title: The Altar of Witness
observations: Upon returning home, the eastern tribes built an altar by the Jordan River. This act raised concerns among the other Israelites, who feared it was a sign of rebellion against God. The altar was intended as a witness to future generations that the eastern tribes were still part of Israel and worshiped the same God.

sections.title: The Response of the Western Tribes
observations: The western tribes, upon hearing of the altar, sent a delegation to confront the eastern tribes. This response highlights the importance of communication and addressing misunderstandings within the community of faith. The western tribes were ready to defend their faith and protect the unity of Israel.

sections.title: Clarification and Reconciliation
observations: The eastern tribes explained their intentions behind building the altar, emphasizing that it was not for sacrifices but as a memorial. This clarification led to reconciliation and a reaffirmation of their shared faith. It serves as a reminder of the need for dialogue and understanding in resolving conflicts.

importantVerses.commentary: The eastern tribes declare their loyalty to God and the unity of Israel, emphasizing that their actions were not meant to separate them from the rest of the nation.
The altar was named 'Ed' which means 'witness', symbolizing the shared faith and commitment of all tribes to serve the Lord.

questions: What does the building of the altar by the eastern tribes reveal about their understanding of identity and community within Israel?
How can we apply the principles of communication and reconciliation seen in this chapter to our own relationships within the church?
What does this chapter teach us about the importance of unity among believers, especially in the face of misunderstandings?
